subtitleEn: It would have been enough for us
heTitleNote: Pesach seder, in the middle of the telling
progression: | Am Am | Dm Am | E E | Am Am |
metaLine: 120 BPM · 4/4 · the loudest thing in the first half of the seder · fifteen steps, each ending on the same word, and the table shouts that word

vocab.da-ye-NU: it would have been enough for us

intro: Fifteen steps out of Egypt, and after each one the table shouts the same word: it would have been enough. Enough for what, exactly, is left unsaid, and that is the argument. The song does not claim that any single step would really have sufficed — you cannot leave Egypt and stop at the edge of the sea. It claims that each one, taken on its own, would have deserved thanks. Grammatically it is the easiest long text in the Haggadah: the same two-clause frame fifteen times, and the second half of one verse becomes the first half of the next.

stanzas.label: how many

lines.en: How many good favours the Place has done for us!
glosses: for the Place, that is, for God

stanzas.summary: {{0.3}} is one of the old names for God, literally "the Place", and it is the one the Haggadah uses here. {{0.1}} means steps or degrees — the favours are being counted as a staircase, which is exactly what the next fifteen verses climb.

stanzas.label: out of Egypt

lines.en: Had He brought us out of Egypt and not carried out judgements against them — enough for us!

stanzas.summary: The frame: if He had done X and not done Y, dayenu. Every following verse takes the Y of this one and makes it the X of the next, so the song is a chain and you always know what comes first.

lines.en: Had He carried out judgements against them and not against their gods — enough for us!
Had He acted against their gods and not killed their firstborn — enough for us!
Had He killed their firstborn and not given us their wealth — enough for us!
Had He given us their wealth and not split the sea for us — enough for us!

stanzas.label: the sea

lines.en: Had He split the sea for us and not brought us through it on dry ground — enough for us!

stanzas.summary: {{6.8}} is dry ground, and it is the detail Exodus insists on: not merely a path, but a dry one. The song keeps the detail.

lines.en: Had He brought us through it on dry ground and not sunk our oppressors in it — enough for us!
Had He sunk our oppressors in it and not supplied our needs in the wilderness for forty years — enough for us!
Had He supplied our needs in the wilderness for forty years and not fed us the manna — enough for us!

stanzas.label: the manna

lines.en: Had He fed us the manna and not given us the Sabbath — enough for us!

stanzas.summary: The Sabbath arrives between food and revelation, before Sinai. In this ordering it is not a commandment given at the mountain; it is something handed over in the desert, with the manna.

lines.en: Had He given us the Sabbath and not brought us before Mount Sinai — enough for us!

stanzas.label: Sinai

lines.en: Had He brought us before Mount Sinai and not given us the Torah — enough for us!

stanzas.summary: Standing at the mountain and receiving what was said there are counted as two separate favours. That separation is the boldest line in the song: arriving would have been enough.

lines.en: Had He given us the Torah and not brought us into the land of Israel — enough for us!

stanzas.label: the land

lines.en: Had He brought us into the land of Israel and not built us the Temple — enough for us!

stanzas.summary: The staircase ends at the Temple, which is the one item on the list that is not standing today. The song counts it anyway, in the past tense, alongside fourteen things that happened.

stanzas.label: all of it together

stichs.en: How much more so, doubled and redoubled, is the goodness of the Place toward us:

that He brought us out of Egypt, and carried out judgements against them, and against their gods, and killed their firstborn, and gave us their wealth, and split the sea for us, and brought us through it on dry ground,
and sank our oppressors in it, and supplied our needs in the wilderness for forty years, and fed us the manna, and gave us the Sabbath, and brought us before Mount Sinai, and gave us the Torah,
and brought us into the land of Israel, and built us the house of the choosing, to atone for all our wrongs.

stanzas.summary: The last verse withdraws the whole argument, politely. Each step alone would have been enough — and He did all of them. Note the grammar shift: the fifteen verses used {{1.0}}, "if", a hypothetical; this one uses {{15.9}}, "that He did", a plain statement of fact. Fifteen verses of counterfactual, then one of indicative.

chantTips: The word {{1.7}} is shouted, not sung, and it is shouted by everyone including the people who are not following the Hebrew. Leave a beat for it.
Many tables sing the word three times at the end of each verse. Some sing it once. Follow the house.
The first half of each verse is the second half of the one before, so a table that has lost its place can always rejoin at the next {{1.0}}.
The final verse is not shouted. It is read or sung straight through, and it is noticeably longer than everything before it — do not let the room start clapping.

about.body: In the Magid section, after the recounting of the plagues and before the explanation of the Passover offering, matzah and bitter herbs. It is the moment the seder stops being a lesson and becomes a party, which is roughly halfway through the evening.

Read strictly, several steps could not have stood alone — the sea without the crossing, Sinai without the Torah. The song is not making a logical claim about sufficiency but a claim about gratitude: that each item deserves its own thanks rather than being absorbed into the total. The final verse then supplies the total anyway.

The number of steps matches other fifteens in the seder — the fifteen sections of the evening, the fifteen Songs of Ascents in Psalms, the fifteen steps of the Temple. Whether that is design or a pattern read in afterwards is not something this page can settle.
